claim: Bmal1 is induced by inflammatory stimulants including Ifn-γ/lipopolysaccharide (M1) in mouse macrophages.
source: We find that the molecular clock Bmal1 is induced by inflammatory stimulants, including Ifn-γ/lipopolysaccharide (M1) and tumor-conditioned medium, to maintain mitochondrial metabolism under metabolically stressed conditions in mouse macrophages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing Bmal1 protein and mRNA levels increase after M1 activation (Figure 1A-C).

claim: Bmal1 is induced by tumor-conditioned medium in mouse macrophages.
source: We find that the molecular clock Bmal1 is induced by inflammatory stimulants, including Ifn-γ/lipopolysaccharide (M1) and tumor-conditioned medium, to maintain mitochondrial metabolism under metabolically stressed conditions in mouse macrophages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing Bmal1 expression increases with tumor-conditioned medium treatment (Figure 6A).

claim: Myeloid-specific Bmal1 knockout renders macrophages unable to sustain mitochondrial function upon M1 stimulation.
source: Upon M1 stimulation, myeloid-specific Bmal1 knockout (M-BKO) renders macrophages unable to sustain mitochondrial function, enhancing succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-mediated mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen species as well as Hif-1α-dependent metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory damage.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced oxygen consumption rate and ETC complex activity in M-BKO macrophages (Figure 2B-C).

claim: Myeloid-specific Bmal1 knockout enhances succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-mediated mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen species.
source: Upon M1 stimulation, myeloid-specific Bmal1 knockout (M-BKO) renders macrophages unable to sustain mitochondrial function, enhancing succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-mediated mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen species as well as Hif-1α-dependent metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory damage.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased mROS levels in M-BKO macrophages (Figure 4C).

claim: Myeloid-specific Bmal1 knockout enhances Hif-1α-dependent metabolic reprogramming.
source: Upon M1 stimulation, myeloid-specific Bmal1 knockout (M-BKO) renders macrophages unable to sustain mitochondrial function, enhancing succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)-mediated mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen species as well as Hif-1α-dependent metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory damage.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing elevated Hif-1α protein levels and increased glycolysis in M-BKO macrophages (Figure 4A, Figure 2E).

claim: Aberrant Hif-1α activation and metabolic dysregulation by M-BKO contribute to an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.
source: In tumor-associated macrophages, aberrant Hif-1α activation and metabolic dysregulation by M-BKO contribute to an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced CD8+ T cell and NK cell populations in tumors co-injected with M-BKO macrophages (Figure 7B).

claim: M-BKO increases melanoma tumor burden.
source: Consequently, M-BKO increases melanoma tumor burden, whereas administering the SDH inhibitor dimethyl malonate suppresses tumor growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased tumor volume in M-BKO mice (Figure 6F, Figure 7A).

claim: Administering the SDH inhibitor dimethyl malonate suppresses melanoma tumor growth.
source: Consequently, M-BKO increases melanoma tumor burden, whereas administering the SDH inhibitor dimethyl malonate suppresses tumor growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced tumor volume with DMM treatment (Figure 7C).

claim: Bmal1 functions as a metabolic checkpoint that integrates macrophage mitochondrial metabolism, redox homeostasis and effector functions.
source: Therefore, Bmal1 functions as a metabolic checkpoint that integrates macrophage mitochondrial metabolism, redox homeostasis and effector functions.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental findings showing Bmal1's role in regulating mitochondrial function, ROS production, and macrophage activation.

claim: The Bmal1-Hif-1α regulatory loop may provide therapeutic opportunities for inflammatory diseases and immunotherapy.
source: This Bmal1-Hif-1α regulatory loop may provide therapeutic opportunities for inflammatory diseases and immunotherapy.
evidence: Based on speculation from the experimental findings showing that targeting this pathway affects tumor growth and inflammation.

claim: Activation of macrophages by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) shifts core metabolic function towards increased reliance on aerobic glycolysis.
source: For instance, activation of macrophages by bacterial products, such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from gram-negative bacteria, shifts core metabolic function towards increased reliance on aerobic glycolysis, with concomitant inhibition of mitochondrial respiration (Fukuzumi et al., 1996; Rodríguez-Prados et al., 2010; Tannahill et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Activation of macrophages by LPS causes concomitant inhibition of mitochondrial respiration.
source: For instance, activation of macrophages by bacterial products, such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from gram-negative bacteria, shifts core metabolic function towards increased reliance on aerobic glycolysis, with concomitant inhibition of mitochondrial respiration (Fukuzumi et al., 1996; Rodríguez-Prados et al., 2010; Tannahill et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Depressed mitochondrial function in activated macrophages leads to the 'broken TCA cycle'.
source: It leads to the so-called 'broken TCA cycle' that results, in part, from the shunting of citric acid to lipid synthesis (Andrejeva and Rathmell, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Itaconate can modulate macrophage immune response through different mechanisms.
source: Itaconate, also derived from citrate/aconitate, can modulate macrophage immune response through different mechanisms (Lampropoulou et al., 2016; Mills et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Succinate accumulates through anaplerotic reactions, notably glutaminolysis, in activated macrophages.
source: By contrast, succinate accumulates through anaplerotic reactions, notably glutaminolysis (Tannahill et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Succinate oxidation to fumarate, mediated by succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)/ETC complex II activity, is a primary source of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mROS) in inflammatory macrophages.
source: Succinate oxidation to fumarate, mediated by succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)/ETC complex II activity, is a primary source of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mROS) in inflammatory macrophages that are involved in bactericidal activity (Mills et al., 2016; West et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: mROS in inflammatory macrophages are involved in bactericidal activity.
source: Succinate oxidation to fumarate, mediated by succinate dehydrogenase (SDH)/ETC complex II activity, is a primary source of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mROS) in inflammatory macrophages that are involved in bactericidal activity (Mills et al., 2016; West et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Succinate/SDH triggers mROS production through accumulation of reduced coenzyme Q leading to reverse electron transfer to ETC complex I.
source: Succinate/SDH is believed to trigger mROS production through accumulation of reduced coenzyme Q leading to reverse electron transfer to ETC complex I (Chouchani et al., 2014; Robb et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: mROS stabilize hypoxia-inducible factor (Hif)-1α through inhibition of prolyl-hydroxylase enzymes.
source: In addition to their bacteria-killing effect, mROS stabilize hypoxia-inducible factor (Hif)-1α through inhibition of prolyl-hydroxylase enzymes that target Hif-1α for ubiquitination by the von Hippel–Lindau (Vhl) E3 ubiquitin ligase and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Bell et al., 2007; Jaakkola et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Prolyl-hydroxylase enzymes target Hif-1α for ubiquitination by the von Hippel–Lindau (Vhl) E3 ubiquitin ligase and subsequent proteasomal degradation.
source: In addition to their bacteria-killing effect, mROS stabilize hypoxia-inducible factor (Hif)-1α through inhibition of prolyl-hydroxylase enzymes that target Hif-1α for ubiquitination by the von Hippel–Lindau (Vhl) E3 ubiquitin ligase and subsequent proteasomal degradation (Bell et al., 2007; Jaakkola et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Hif-1α is a master transcriptional regulator of genes involved in glycolysis and anabolic metabolism.
source: Hif-1α is a master transcriptional regulator of genes involved in glycolysis and anabolic metabolism, thereby supplementing the energetic needs of the broken TCA cycle (Cramer et al., 2003; Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Semenza et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Hif-1α is required for the expression of the urea cycle enzyme arginase-1 (Arg1).
source: Hif-1α is also required for the expression of the urea cycle enzyme arginase-1 (Arg1).
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about Hif-1α regulation of Arg1.

claim: M1 activation upregulates Arg1 through Hif-1α.
source: However, M1 activation also upregulates Arg1 through Hif-1α.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing Arg1 expression is enhanced in M-BKO macrophages with elevated Hif-1α (Figure 4B).

claim: Tumor-derived lactate increases Hif-1α activity in tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs).
source: Similarly, in the nutrient-deprived tumor microenvironment, tumor-derived lactate has been proposed to increase Hif-1α activity in tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and thus to upregulate Arg1 (Colegio et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Aberrant expression of Arg1 in TAMs results in local arginine depletion that inhibits antitumor immunity mediated by cytotoxic T cells and natural killer (NK) cells.
source: Aberrant expression of Arg1 in TAMs results in local arginine depletion that inhibits antitumor immunity mediated by cytotoxic T cells and natural killer (NK) cells (Doedens et al., 2010; Steggerda et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Myeloid-specific deletion of Hif1a suppresses tumor growth in mice.
source: Accordingly, myeloid-specific deletion of Hif1a or Arg1 suppresses tumor growth in mice (Colegio et al., 2014; Doedens et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Myeloid-specific deletion of Arg1 suppresses tumor growth in mice.
source: Accordingly, myeloid-specific deletion of Hif1a or Arg1 suppresses tumor growth in mice (Colegio et al., 2014; Doedens et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The circadian rhythm has been implicated in the immune response.
source: The circadian rhythm has been implicated in many biological and pathological processes, including the immune response and tumor progression (Hardin and Panda, 2013; Nguyen et al., 2013; Papagiannakopoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The circadian rhythm has been implicated in tumor progression.
source: The circadian rhythm has been implicated in many biological and pathological processes, including the immune response and tumor progression (Hardin and Panda, 2013; Nguyen et al., 2013; Papagiannakopoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: The molecular clock includes the master regulator Bmal1 and its transcriptional partner Clock.
source: The molecular clock includes the master regulator Bmal1 (or Aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator-like protein 1, Arntl) and its transcriptional partner Clock, as well as the negative regulatory loop that includes Nr1d1, Nr1d2, period (Per1/2/3) and cryptochrome (Cry1/2) proteins, and the positive regulator loop that includes Rorα/β/γ (Hardin and Panda, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The molecular clock includes a negative regulatory loop that includes Nr1d1, Nr1d2, period (Per1/2/3) and cryptochrome (Cry1/2) proteins.
source: The molecular clock includes the master regulator Bmal1 (or Aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator-like protein 1, Arntl) and its transcriptional partner Clock, as well as the negative regulatory loop that includes Nr1d1, Nr1d2, period (Per1/2/3) and cryptochrome (Cry1/2) proteins, and the positive regulator loop that includes Rorα/β/γ (Hardin and Panda, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The molecular clock includes a positive regulator loop that includes Rorα/β/γ.
source: The molecular clock includes the master regulator Bmal1 (or Aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator-like protein 1, Arntl) and its transcriptional partner Clock, as well as the negative regulatory loop that includes Nr1d1, Nr1d2, period (Per1/2/3) and cryptochrome (Cry1/2) proteins, and the positive regulator loop that includes Rorα/β/γ (Hardin and Panda, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Pparα, Pparδ/β and Pparγ are downstream of Bmal1/Clock and control the expression of clock output genes.
source: Several nuclear receptors, such as the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors, Pparα, Pparδ/β and Pparγ, are downstream of Bmal1/Clock and control the expression of clock output genes (Canaple et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Time-restricted feeding in mice can synchronize the peripheral clock separately from the central clock.
source: It has been demonstrated that time-restricted feeding in mice can synchronize the peripheral clock separately from the central clock (Damiola et al., 2000), suggesting that a primary function of circadian rhythm is to maximize metabolic efficiency.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: A primary function of circadian rhythm is to maximize metabolic efficiency.
source: It has been demonstrated that time-restricted feeding in mice can synchronize the peripheral clock separately from the central clock (Damiola et al., 2000), suggesting that a primary function of circadian rhythm is to maximize metabolic efficiency.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that feeding can synchronize peripheral clocks.

claim: Hepatic Bmal1 regulates rhythmic mitochondrial capacity in anticipation of nutrient availability.
source: In concert, we and others have shown that hepatic Bmal1 regulates rhythmic mitochondrial capacity in anticipation of nutrient availability (Jacobi et al., 2015; Peek et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work including authors' own work.

claim: Myeloid-specific Bmal1 deletion disrupts diurnal monocyte trafficking.
source: Notably, myeloid-specific Bmal1 deletion disrupts diurnal monocyte trafficking and increases systemic inflammation and mortality in sepsis mouse models (Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Myeloid-specific Bmal1 deletion increases systemic inflammation and mortality in sepsis mouse models.
source: Notably, myeloid-specific Bmal1 deletion disrupts diurnal monocyte trafficking and increases systemic inflammation and mortality in sepsis mouse models (Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: M1 activation caused a progressive decrease in mitochondrial content in WT macrophages.
source: In WT macrophages, M1 activation caused a progressive decrease in mitochondrial content, which was more pronounced in M-BKO macrophages (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing decreased Mitotracker Green staining over time (Figure 2A).

claim: The decrease in mitochondrial content caused by M1 activation was more pronounced in M-BKO macrophages compared to WT.
source: In WT macrophages, M1 activation caused a progressive decrease in mitochondrial content, which was more pronounced in M-BKO macrophages (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing greater reduction in Mitotracker Green staining in M-BKO cells (Figure 2A).

claim: The reduced mitochondrial content in M1-activated macrophages was accompanied by elevated protein levels of the mitophagy receptor Bnip3.
source: The reduced mitochondrial content was accompanied by elevated protein levels of the mitophagy receptor Bnip3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased Bnip3 protein by Western blot (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: M-BKO caused a significant reduction in the activities of complexes II and III in isolated mitochondria 6 hr after M1 stimulation.
source: Measurement of ETC complex activity in isolated mitochondria indicated that M-BKO caused a significant reduction in the activities of complexes II and III, given an equal amount of mitochondrial protein, 6 hr after M1 stimulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced complex II and III activities (Figure 2C).

claim: There was no genotypic difference in the OCR at the resting state between WT and M-BKO macrophages.
source: There was no genotypic difference in the OCR at the resting state, and serum shock did not affect respiration in WT and M-BKO macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Seahorse Mito Stress test (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Serum shock did not affect respiration in WT and M-BKO macrophages.
source: There was no genotypic difference in the OCR at the resting state, and serum shock did not affect respiration in WT and M-BKO macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Seahorse Mito Stress test (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The basal OCR of M-BKO macrophages remained suppressed 24 hr following acute LPS treatment, whereas the basal OCR was completely recovered in WT macrophages.
source: By contrast, the basal OCR of M-BKO macrophages remained suppressed 24 hr following acute LPS treatment, whereas the basal OCR was completely recovered in WT macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Seahorse Mito Stress test (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: LPS injection increased the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) of WT macrophages.
source: Seahorse extracellular flux analysis showed that LPS injection increased the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR, indicative of lactic acid secretion) and decreased the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of WT macrophages, as expected from aerobic glycolysis (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Seahorse extracellular flux analysis (Figure 2D).

claim: LPS injection decreased the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of WT macrophages.
source: Seahorse extracellular flux analysis showed that LPS injection increased the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR, indicative of lactic acid secretion) and decreased the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of WT macrophages, as expected from aerobic glycolysis (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Seahorse extracellular flux analysis (Figure 2D).

claim: The ECAR and OCR were further enhanced and suppressed, respectively, in M-BKO macrophages compared to WT after LPS injection.
source: The ECAR and OCR were further enhanced and suppressed, respectively, in M-BKO macrophages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Seahorse extracellular flux analysis (Figure 2D).

claim: Stable overexpression of Bmal1 in RAW264.7 macrophages resulted in higher OCR and lower ECAR after LPS stimulation, compared to control cells.
source: By contrast, stable overexpression of Bmal1 (Bmal1-OE) in RAW264.7 macrophages resulted in higher OCR and lower ECAR after LPS stimulation, compared to control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Seahorse extracellular flux analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G).

claim: There was no difference in the basal glycolytic rate between WT and M-BKO macrophages.
source: There was no difference in the basal glycolytic rate between WT and M-BKO macrophages (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from glycolytic stress test (Figure 2E).

claim: LPS increased ECAR in both WT and M-BKO macrophages and to a greater extent in M-BKO macrophages.
source: LPS increased ECAR in both genotypes and to a greater extent in M-BKO macrophages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from glycolytic stress test (Figure 2E).

claim: An increase in the glycolytic rate was observed in splenic macrophages from M-BKO mice isolated 6 hr after i.p. injection of LPS.
source: Furthermore, an increase in the glycolytic rate was observed in splenic macrophages from M-BKO mice isolated 6 hr after i.p. injection of LPS, which was accompanied by lowered circulating glucose levels, indicative of increased glucose consumption by inflammatory myeloid cells in M-BKO mice when compared to WT animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from glycolytic stress test on splenic macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-I).

claim: Lowered circulating glucose levels were observed in M-BKO mice 6 hr after i.p. injection of LPS, indicative of increased glucose consumption by inflammatory myeloid cells.
source: Furthermore, an increase in the glycolytic rate was observed in splenic macrophages from M-BKO mice isolated 6 hr after i.p. injection of LPS, which was accompanied by lowered circulating glucose levels, indicative of increased glucose consumption by inflammatory myeloid cells in M-BKO mice when compared to WT animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced blood glucose levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-I).

claim: M1 activation caused accumulation of glycolytic intermediates (glucose-6-phosphate, fructose-6-phosphate and lactic acid) in macrophages.
source: As has been reported (Tannahill et al., 2013), M1 activation caused accumulation of glycolytic intermediates (glucose-6-phosphate, fructose-6-phosphate and lactic acid) and depletion of TCA metabolites (e.g. citrate) but accumulation of succinate.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3A-B) and citation to prior work.

claim: M1 activation caused depletion of TCA metabolites (e.g. citrate) in macrophages.
source: As has been reported (Tannahill et al., 2013), M1 activation caused accumulation of glycolytic intermediates (glucose-6-phosphate, fructose-6-phosphate and lactic acid) and depletion of TCA metabolites (e.g. citrate) but accumulation of succinate.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3A-B) and citation to prior work.

claim: Glycolytic metabolites and succinate were significantly higher in M-BKO macrophages than in WT cells after M1 activation.
source: Glycolytic metabolites and succinate were significantly higher in M-BKO macrophages than in WT cells.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3A-B).

claim: M-BKO cells showed accumulation of several amino acids and intermediates of the urea cycle after M1 activation.
source: M-BKO cells also showed accumulation of several amino acids and intermediates of the urea cycle (which detoxifies ammonia released from amino-acid deamination) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data (Figure 3A).

claim: M1-stimulated glucose uptake was higher in M-BKO macrophages than in WT cells.
source: Consistent with the increased glycolytic metabolites, M1-stimulated glucose uptake and lactate production were higher in M-BKO macrophages than in WT cells (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data measuring glucose uptake (Figure 3C).

claim: M1-stimulated lactate production was higher in M-BKO macrophages than in WT cells.
source: Consistent with the increased glycolytic metabolites, M1-stimulated glucose uptake and lactate production were higher in M-BKO macrophages than in WT cells (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data measuring lactate secretion (Figure 3D).

claim: M1 activation led to a several-fold induction of Hif-1α protein levels in M-BKO macrophages compared to WT cells.
source: Western blot analyses revealed that M1 activation led to a several-fold induction of Hif-1α protein levels in M-BKO macrophages compared to WT cells (Figure 4A), whereas Bmal1-OE RAW264.7 macrophages showed reduced Hif-1α protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot (Figure 4A).

claim: Bmal1-OE RAW264.7 macrophages showed reduced Hif-1α protein after M1 activation.
source: Western blot analyses revealed that M1 activation led to a several-fold induction of Hif-1α protein levels in M-BKO macrophages compared to WT cells (Figure 4A), whereas Bmal1-OE RAW264.7 macrophages showed reduced Hif-1α protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The expression of Hif-1α targets Ldha, Arg1 and Il1b was enhanced by M-BKO and blocked by myeloid Hif1a knockout (M-HKO).
source: The expression of Hif-1α targets, such as lactate dehydrogenase A (Ldha), Arg1 and Il1b, was enhanced by M-BKO and blocked by myeloid Hif1a knockout (M-HKO, Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from qPCR (Figure 4B).

claim: Hif-1α gene expression did not differ between WT and M-BKO cells.
source: Hif-1α gene expression did not differ between WT and M-BKO cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from qPCR (Figure 1D).

claim: Levels of mROS were higher in isolated mitochondria from M-BKO macrophages at 1 hr and 4 hr of M1 activation than in WT macrophages.
source: In fact, levels of mROS were higher in isolated mitochondria from M-BKO macrophages at 1 hr and 4 hr of M1 activation than in WT macrophages (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data measuring mROS with MitoSox Red (Figure 4C).

claim: The addition of succinate increased mROS production in mitochondria from both WT and M-BKO macrophages.
source: The addition of succinate increased mROS production in mitochondria from both WT and M-BKO macrophages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data measuring mROS with MitoSox Red (Figure 4C).

claim: An additional two-fold induction of mROS was detected in mitochondria from 4-hr M1-stimulated M-BKO, but not in those from WT macrophages, after succinate addition.
source: An additional two-fold induction of mROS was detected in mitochondria from 4-hr M1-stimulated M-BKO, but not in those from WT macrophages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data measuring mROS with MitoSox Red (Figure 4C).

claim: Hif-1α protein accumulation could be normalized between genotypes by co-treatment with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (N-AC).
source: Hif-1α protein accumulation could be normalized between genotypes by co-treatment with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (N-AC) or the competitive complex II inhibitor dimethylmalonate (DMM), which blocks mROS production (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot (Figure 4D).

claim: Hif-1α protein accumulation could be normalized between genotypes by co-treatment with the competitive complex II inhibitor dimethylmalonate (DMM), which blocks mROS production.
source: Hif-1α protein accumulation could be normalized between genotypes by co-treatment with the antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (N-AC) or the competitive complex II inhibitor dimethylmalonate (DMM), which blocks mROS production (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot (Figure 4D).

claim: M1-stimulated glucose uptake was attenuated in myeloid-specific Bmal1 and Hif1a double knockout macrophages (M-BHdKO).
source: Furthermore, M1-stimulated glucose uptake, lactate release and aerobic glycolysis were attenuated in myeloid-specific Bmal1 and Hif1a double knockout macrophages (M-BHdKO; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D), indicating that the increased glucose utilization in M-BKO was Hif-1α-dependent.
evidence: Supported by experimental data measuring glucose uptake (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: M1-stimulated lactate release was attenuated in myeloid-specific Bmal1 and Hif1a double knockout macrophages (M-BHdKO).
source: Furthermore, M1-stimulated glucose uptake, lactate release and aerobic glycolysis were attenuated in myeloid-specific Bmal1 and Hif1a double knockout macrophages (M-BHdKO; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D), indicating that the increased glucose utilization in M-BKO was Hif-1α-dependent.
evidence: Supported by experimental data measuring lactate secretion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: M1-stimulated aerobic glycolysis was attenuated in myeloid-specific Bmal1 and Hif1a double knockout macrophages (M-BHdKO).
source: Furthermore, M1-stimulated glucose uptake, lactate release and aerobic glycolysis were attenuated in myeloid-specific Bmal1 and Hif1a double knockout macrophages (M-BHdKO; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D), indicating that the increased glucose utilization in M-BKO was Hif-1α-dependent.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from glycolytic stress test (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).

claim: The increased glucose utilization in M-BKO was Hif-1α-dependent.
source: Furthermore, M1-stimulated glucose uptake, lactate release and aerobic glycolysis were attenuated in myeloid-specific Bmal1 and Hif1a double knockout macrophages (M-BHdKO; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D), indicating that the increased glucose utilization in M-BKO was Hif-1α-dependent.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that double knockout normalizes glucose utilization.

claim: Expression of Nfe2l2- and Nrf2-induced oxidative stress responsive genes, such as NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (Nqo1), were upregulated in M-BKO macrophages upon M1 stimulation.
source: However, we found that expression of Nfe2l2- and Nrf2-induced oxidative stress responsive genes, such as NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (Nqo1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), were upregulated in M-BKO macrophages upon M1 stimulation, suggesting that increased mROS associated with M-BKO was the cause rather than the consequence of dysregulated Nrf2 signaling.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from qPCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Increased mROS associated with M-BKO was the cause rather than the consequence of dysregulated Nrf2 signaling.
source: However, we found that expression of Nfe2l2- and Nrf2-induced oxidative stress responsive genes, such as NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1 (Nqo1; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), were upregulated in M-BKO macrophages upon M1 stimulation, suggesting that increased mROS associated with M-BKO was the cause rather than the consequence of dysregulated Nrf2 signaling.
evidence: Based on inference from the observation that Nrf2 target genes are upregulated in M-BKO.

claim: Bmal1 and Hif-1α regulate opposing metabolic programs.
source: These data indicate that Bmal1 and Hif-1α regulate opposing metabolic programs and that Bmal1-mediated mitochondrial metabolism serves to fine-tune Hif-1α activity by modulating oxidative stress.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental observations showing opposite effects on metabolism.

claim: Bmal1-mediated mitochondrial metabolism serves to fine-tune Hif-1α activity by modulating oxidative stress.
source: These data indicate that Bmal1 and Hif-1α regulate opposing metabolic programs and that Bmal1-mediated mitochondrial metabolism serves to fine-tune Hif-1α activity by modulating oxidative stress.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations showing Bmal1 affects mROS and Hif-1α levels.

claim: The majority of M1-induced or -suppressed genes were regulated in a similar manner in WT and M-BKO macrophages.
source: These analyses revealed that the majority of M1-induced or -suppressed genes were regulated in a similar manner in WT and M-BKO macrophages, suggesting that Bmal1 gene deletion affected specific inflammatory processes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—source data 1) and in line with the intact expression pattern of Nfkb1 in M-BKO macrophages (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Bmal1 gene deletion affected specific inflammatory processes.
source: These analyses revealed that the majority of M1-induced or -suppressed genes were regulated in a similar manner in WT and M-BKO macrophages, suggesting that Bmal1 gene deletion affected specific inflammatory processes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—source data 1) and in line with the intact expression pattern of Nfkb1 in M-BKO macrophages (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on inference from RNA-seq data showing selective gene expression changes.

claim: Most TCA cycle enzymes were downregulated by M1 activation.
source: In the carbohydrate metabolism category, most TCA cycle enzymes were downregulated by M1 activation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 5A).

claim: Direct comparison between M1-stimulated WT and M-BKO macrophages identified 419 genes that are more highly expressed in M1-activated M-BKO macrophages.
source: Direct comparison between M1-stimulated WT and M-BKO macrophages identified 419 genes that are more highly expressed in M1-activated M-BKO macrophages (FDR < 0.05, p<0.05, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Most-enriched categories of genes more highly expressed in M1-activated M-BKO macrophages included stress and inflammatory responses.
source: Most-enriched categories included stress and inflammatory responses that contained Il1b and other Hif-1α target genes, such as S100a8/S100a9 (Grebhardt et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data and citation.

claim: Other top enriched pathways in genes more highly expressed in M1-activated M-BKO macrophages were protein catabolism and amino-acid transport.
source: Other top enriched pathways were protein catabolism and amino-acid transport.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.
